ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The University of Kansas Institutional Review Board approved the study procedures (IRB: STUDY00151870).
We recruited participants through the University of Kansas Psychology participant pool and with flyers posted on campus and in the surrounding community.
To be eligible, participants had to be English-speaking and between 18 and 45 years old.
Participants gave informed consent before the study began.

The final sample included 16 participants (9 female, 7 male), ranging in age from 18 to 24 years (M = 20.06), and recruited from the University of Kansas psychology participant pool (n = 12) or the local community (n = 4).
After being fitted with both devices, participants completed 7 tasks in a fixed order: baseline, breathing, picture viewing, walking, squats, typing, and instruction following.
Fourth, participants completed 3 minutes of walking back and forth in the lab.
Fifth, participants completed 30 body-weights squats, which includes movement along the y-axis.
In the seventh task, participants were presented with a series of instructions to follow (for 30 seconds each) on a computer screen.
The initial instructions were "neutral" tasks, such as "think of animals starting with the letter P." Then, unexpectedly, participants were told they had 30 seconds to prepare a song to sing.
Participants completed seven tasks in a fixed order, including baseline measures, and psychological and physical stressors (inspired by Menghini et al., 2019).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Consumer wearable devices, like smartwatches, may offer a more practical way to collect cardiac data in everyday life.
Yet, to be used in a research study, prior work suggests comparing the accuracy of smartwatches against a gold-standard electrocardiography (ECG) device across various conditions.
In the present work, we tested the accuracy of the Garmin Vivosmart 5, a wrist-worn smartwatch, against the research-grade Mindware Mobile ECG in collecting heart period data.
Participants wore both devices as they completed 7 tasks, including physical and psychological stressors.

We assessed how closely the two devices' heart period estimates agreed within each task, the magnitude and direction of the differences between devices, and whether the two devices detected the same task-related changes from baseline task estimates.
Agreement between the devices was assessed using absolute-agreement intraclass correlations (ICCs) for each task.
We found that agreement was good to excellent during seated tasks (ICC = 889 -.997), but poor during movement tasks (ICCs < .2).
text.formatted: We found that agreement was good to excellent during seated tasks (ICC = 889 -.997), but poor during movement tasks (ICCs < .2).

text.text: Averaged across all tasks and participants, the differences in heart period between Garmin and MindWare was small and not significant, M = 12.3 ms, 95% CI [-8.6, 33.3].

However, we also found that the magnitude and direction of the differences between Garmin and MindWare were significantly different across tasks, F (6, 85.4) = 5.16, p < .001, with the largest differences occurring during the movement tasks.
text.formatted: However, we also found that the magnitude and direction of the differences between Garmin and MindWare were significantly different across tasks, F (6, 85.4) = 5.16, p < .001, with the largest differences occurring during the movement tasks.

text.text: Our findings suggest that the Garmin Vivosmart 5 can reliably estimate heart period (provide similar heart period estimates to the Mindware ECG) especially during seated tasks, while tasks with heavy movement present larger discrepancies that should be accounted for.
Electrocardiography (ECG) has long been the gold standard for measuring cardiac activity in psychophysiological research.

By recording the heart's electrical activity via electrodes placed on the chest, ECG captures each cardiac cycle, from which heart rate, heart-rate variability, and related measures can be derived (Quigley et al., 2024).
text.formatted: By recording the heart's electrical activity via electrodes placed on the chest, ECG captures each cardiac cycle, from which heart rate, heart-rate variability, and related measures can be derived <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Quigley et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: ECG is noninvasive, inexpensive, and relatively easy to use in clinical and research settings.
Outside of the lab, however, keeping electrodes and leads in place on a moving person is difficult, and the signal quality becomes more noisy as a result.
Wrist-worn devices (e.g., smartwatches and fitness bands) are now used by millions of adults, and they may offer a more practical way to collect cardiac data (Haridas et al., 2026).

text.text: These devices are easy to set up and comfortable to wear all day, allowing researchers to track cardiac activity repeatedly and over longer periods (e.g., weeks instead of a single lab session).
Cardiac recordings can also be paired with ecological momentary assessment (EMA), linking how people are feeling to their physiology (Hoemann et al., 2020; Karimi et al., 2024; Tutunji et al., 2023).

text.text: We sought out to test the utility of one wrist-worn smartwatch, the Garmin Vívosmart® 5, a fitness tracker made to monitor daily health, sleep, and workouts (Garmin, 2022).

text.text: We compare the Garmin Vívosmart to the research-grade MindWare Mobile ECG (MindWare Technologies, 2014).

text.text: Our goal with this project was to see how similar the two devices perform across a variety of tasks, including some that were psychologically stressful or physically demanding.
In the present study, the cardiac measure of interest is heart period, or the time between heartbeats, averaged within 30-second periods.
It is important to note that the MindWare and Garmin devices derive heart period in different ways.

The MindWare Mobile ECG measures the heart's electrical activity and produces a complete heartbeat waveform, including the P wave (depolarization of the left atrium), the QRS complex ( depolarization of ventricles), and the T wave (repolarization of ventricles) (Quigley et al., 2024).

text.text: Heart period from the ECG is measured as the R-R interval, or the time between the peaks of successive R waves.
The Garmin Vívosmart 5, in contrast, relies on wrist photoplethysmography (PPG).

The watch shines a light onto the wrist, and with each heartbeat, different amounts of reflected light correspond to blood flow changes that are recorded as beat-by-beat pulses (Nelson et al., 2020; Quigley et al., 2024).

Differences between devices were small and not significant for the baseline (16.2 ms), paced breathing (18.1 ms), and picture viewing (2.6 ms) tasks.

In contrast, the Garmin estimated significantly longer heart periods (i.e., slower heart rate) during typing, mean difference = 34.1 ms, 95% CI [15.5, 52.6], t(13) = 3.96, p = .011, and instruction following, mean difference = 35.1 ms, 95% CI [13.8, 56.5], t(14) = 3.53, p = .020.

The largest mean differences occurred during the movement tasks (walking and squats): Garmin heart periods were 71.0 ms shorter (i.e., faster heart rate) during walking, 95% CI [-144.6, 2.5], t(14) = -2.07, p = .287, and 51.7 ms longer (i.e., slower heart rate) during squats, 95% CI [-13.0, 116.5], t(15) = 1.70, p = .344.

Looking at the confidence intervals, we can note a larger standard deviation of the differences for the movement tasks (125.99 ms for walking and 124.62 ms for squats), compared with 9.01 to 42.56 ms across the seated tasks (see Figure 7).
text.formatted: Looking at the confidence intervals, we can note a larger standard deviation of the differences for the movement tasks (125.99 ms for walking and 124.62 ms for squats), compared with 9.01 to 42.56 ms across the seated tasks (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">7</ref>).

text.text: In summary, the results of the ICCs and linear mixed-effects model suggest larger differences between devices for the movement tasks (see discussion for additional thoughts on this).
Finally, we asked whether the two devices detected the same task-related changes in heart period compared to an individual's baseline heart period.
As expected, both devices recorded shorter heart periods (i.e., faster heart rate) during walking and squats compared to baseline.

MindWare heart period was, on average, 60.5 ms shorter than baseline during walking, p = .022, and 192.8 ms shorter during squats, p < .001; Garmin heart period was, on average, 147.7 ms shorter during walking and 157.3 ms shorter during squats, both ps < .001, see discussion for thoughts on these differences.
text.formatted: MindWare heart period was, on average, 60.5 ms shorter than baseline during walking, p = .022, and 192.8 ms shorter during squats, p < .001; Garmin heart period was, on average, 147.7 ms shorter during walking and 157.3 ms shorter during squats, both ps < .001, see discussion for thoughts on these differences.

text.text: During typing and instruction following, both devices showed decreases in heart period (i.e., faster heart rate): MindWare typing was -68.8 ms shorter (p = .011) and instruction following was -69.0 ms shorter (p = .011), wheras Garmin was -50.9 and -50.1 ms shorter respecively ( both p values were not significant).
Neither device showed a significant change from baseline, on average, during paced breathing or picture viewing, which may be the result of the tasks being at seated rest (see Figure 8).
text.formatted: Neither device showed a significant change from baseline, on average, during paced breathing or picture viewing, which may be the result of the tasks being at seated rest (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">8</ref>).

text.text: Heart Period Changes From Baseline
In the analyses above, we averaged heart period within each task across participants, but we also wanted to explore agreement between devices at the participant level.
To do so, following recommendations from van Lier et al. (2020), we created timecourse plots of each participant's 30-second heart period estimates from both devices across the session.

We also created a Bland-Altman plot for each participant to examine bias in heart period across the devices (the mean Garmin minus MindWare difference across paired 30-second bins and the 95% limits of agreement (bias ± 1.96 standard deviations of the differences), organized by task (Bland & Altman, 1986).
text.formatted: We also created a Bland-Altman plot for each participant to examine bias in heart period across the devices (the mean Garmin minus MindWare difference across paired 30-second bins and the 95% limits of agreement (bias ± 1.96 standard deviations of the differences), organized by task <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bland & Altman, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: We present two examples of participants who completed all seven tasks.
Participant GM1018 (Figure 9; 42 paired 30-second bins) had long resting heart periods (roughly 1,000 to 1,100 ms/55-60 beats per minute).
text.formatted: Participant GM1018 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">9</ref>; 42 paired 30-second bins) had long resting heart periods (roughly 1,000 to 1,100 ms/55-60 beats per minute).

text.text: Their average bias between devices was 20.4 ms, with 95% limits of agreement from -75.2 to 116.0 ms.
Looking at GM1018's timecourse figure, we see excellent agreement across the two devices' heart period estimates during almost all of the tasks (with the exception of the squats task).
Similarly, in the Bland-Altman plot, the two squats bins had the largest differences (at or above the upper limit of agreement).

Overall, we should be confident in both the Garmin and MindWare estimates of heart period for this participant as the devices have good agreement and only one bin is outside of the limits of agreement on the Bland-Altman plot.
In contrast, participant GM1020 (Figure 10; 43 paired 30-second bins) showed larger discrepancies between devices, especially for the movement tasks.
text.formatted: In contrast, participant GM1020 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">10</ref>; 43 paired 30-second bins) showed larger discrepancies between devices, especially for the movement tasks.

text.text: The average bias between devices was -57.8 ms, with larger 95% limits of agreement from -459.7 to 344.1 ms.

For participant GM1020, the timecourse figure shows good agreement for most of the tasks, however, the devices diverge slightly in the heart period estimates during the baseline and breathing tasks, and substantially during the walking and squats tasks.
GM1020's Bland-Altman figure shows the extreme bias during the walking task where multiple 30-second bins are outside the limits of agreement.
In cases like this, researchers should consider removing 30-second bins with extreme bias.
In this case, MindWare estimated heart periods that were longer than baseline (i.e., slower heart rate) during a task that involved physical activity where heart rate would be faster.
One reason this may have occured is due to the MindWare ECG leads moving a lot during a physical task and creating noise in the estimates (more on this in the discussion section).
The Garmin Vívosmart 5 agreed well with the MindWare ECG when participants completed stationary or seated tasks, however, the devices disagreed more during movement tasks.
More specifically, ICCs for average heart period ranged from .889 to .997 across the five seated tasks and were near zero during walking and squats.

This matches earlier validation work on wrist-worn PPG devices, which tend to agree more with ECG during rest and disagree during tasks with heavy movement (Menghini et al., 2019; Nelson et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This matches earlier validation work on wrist-worn PPG devices, which tend to agree more with ECG during rest and disagree during tasks with heavy movement <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Menghini et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Nelson et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These validation study findings also show why devices need to be tested across several conditions (Kleckner et al., 2021; Menghini et al., 2019; van Lier et al., 2020).
text.formatted: These validation study findings also show why devices need to be tested across several conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Kleckner et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Menghini et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">van Lier et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: One potential reason for the discrepancies during movement tasks is that the MindWare ECG could be more affected by movement due to the electrode wires.
The electrode leads in our study were not taped down and participants' clothing and body movements may have affected the data collection and ECG signal quality.
For example, some participants wore clothing with loose elastic waistbands, or engaged in more exaggerated physical movement, even while seated.
Additionally, the MindWare data used here were not manually cleaned, so there may be additional outliers in the MindWare data that can be accounted for.
However, because the Garmin data cannot be cleaned (the raw PPG signal is not retained), here we chose to focus on a comparison of raw signals.
Movement can also disrupt wrist PPG estimates (Nelson et al., 2020), and, as a result, it is not apparent which device is "more accurate" at estimating heart period during movement tasks.
text.formatted: Movement can also disrupt wrist PPG estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Nelson et al., 2020)</ref>, and, as a result, it is not apparent which device is "more accurate" at estimating heart period during movement tasks.

text.text: Another possible explanation for some of the discrepancies is that the Garmin may have difficulty capturing rapid changes in heart period.
For example, participant GM1018 showed relatively good agreement across most 30-second bins, with 29 of 42 bins differing by less than 50 ms.

However, some of the largest differences occurred during the squats task (which was a shorter task) and in the final bins of instruction following (when participants were completing the sing-a-song stressor), when heart period was shortening quickly.

In most of these bins, the Garmin estimated longer heart periods (e.g., slower heart rate) than the MindWare, which may suggest that the MindWare is able to pick up on more subtle changes in heart period.
Another possibility is that the Garmin misses or smooths over some beats when the wrist is moving or heart period is changing rapidly.
However, Garmin uses proprietary processing algorithms, and we do not have access to the raw PPG signal (Garmin Health, 2023).
text.formatted: However, Garmin uses proprietary processing algorithms, and we do not have access to the raw PPG signal <ref type="bibr">(Garmin Health, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: It is therefore difficult to determine whether these differences were due to smoothing, missed beats, or other sources of measurement error.
Future validation studies could assess how closely the Vívosmart 5 tracks rapid changes in heart period during psychological and physical stressors.
Access to raw PPG recordings from Garmin would allow researchers to synchronize the PPG waveform with the raw MindWare ECG for a more precise comparison of the signals.
If raw PPG recordings cannot be shared, Garmin researchers could conduct their own validation study and report agreement with a research-grade ECG for psychological and physical stressors.
One takeaway from our work is that the Garmin Vívosmart 5 may be suitable for some research questions but not others.

For studies that pair wearable recordings with EMA in daily life (Hoemann et al., 2020; Tutunji et al., 2023), our results support using the Garmin to estimate average heart period, especially during tasks where people are sitting still.
text.formatted: For studies that pair wearable recordings with EMA in daily life <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Hoemann et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Tutunji et al., 2023)</ref>, our results support using the Garmin to estimate average heart period, especially during tasks where people are sitting still.

text.text: However, the larger discrepancies observed during full-body movement tasks suggest that, during physical activity, we should interpret heart period estimates with caution.
The watch may also be less suitable for studies interested in rapid or short-term changes in heart period, although we did not directly test its temporal precision.

One option for future studies would be to use movement data from the watch's accelerometer or a smartphone to identify periods of intense movement and account for them in subsequent analyses (Hoemann et al., 2020).
text.formatted: One option for future studies would be to use movement data from the watch's accelerometer or a smartphone to identify periods of intense movement and account for them in subsequent analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Hoemann et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We also recognize several limitations to our study.
First, we only examined average heart period here, so our findings may not generalize to heart rate variability or other cardiorespiratory measures that are available on the Garmin Vívosmart 5.

Second, we tested the devices across a limited number of laboratory tasks, which may not parallel how they perform during daily life, which may present other challenges with physical acclivity, moisture, or sweating.
Finally, future validation studies could examine whether agreement during movement improves when ECG electrode wires are taped down and movement artifacts are manually corrected.

Despite these limitations, our results suggest that the Garmin Vívosmart 5 is a good option for estimating average heart period during seated activities, but additional validation is needed before relying on it during movement tasks or for detecting rapid changes in heart period.
